abstract: BLS Employment Situation for October 2026, released November 6, 2026. Total nonfarm payroll employment rose 165,000 and the unemployment rate was little changed at 4.1 percent. The gain ran well above the 48,000 average of the prior 12 months, and August and September were both revised up, for a combined 84,000 more than first reported - reversing the 60,000 downward revision carried in the September release. Professional and business services, the sector closest to the white-collar displacement thesis, added 70,000 and has now recovered 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 2025.
keyFindings: Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, 'higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the prior 12 months' - the strongest month of a weak year rather than a continuation of it.
The unemployment rate was little changed at 4.1 percent, with 7.1 million unemployed, and has held in a narrow 4.1 to 4.3 percent range.

August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 to +186,000, and September up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000; combined, the two months are 84,000 higher than previously reported. The direction of revisions flipped from the September release, where July and August had been cut by 60,000 combined.

Professional and business services increased by 70,000, against a 12-month average of 15,000 per month, and 'has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 2025.' Within it, professional, scientific and technical services rose 33,000 and administrative and support 28,000.
Information employment showed little change over the month at -1,000, and financial activities little change at +7,000. Both sectors remain the ones to watch for AI displacement, and neither moved.
Health care added 42,000 against a 31,000 12-month average, transportation and warehousing 25,000, and manufacturing 19,000, including 7,000 in computer and electronic product manufacturing.
Average hourly earnings rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00, and 3.1 percent over the year - a slight acceleration from the 3.0 percent 12-month figure in the September report.
methodology: Two monthly surveys run by the Census Bureau for BLS: the establishment survey (Current Employment Statistics, about 119,000 businesses and government agencies) for payroll employment, hours and earnings by industry, and the household survey (Current Population Survey, about 60,000 households) for the unemployment rate and labor force status by demographic group. Payroll estimates are revised in each of the two months following first publication as more establishment reports arrive, and the household survey is not revised monthly.
qualifiers: Tier 1 official statistics, but an aggregate measure that cannot attribute employment change to AI. It is the denominator against which AI-specific displacement claims are checked, not evidence of AI's effect in either direction: a strong month does not disprove AI displacement and a weak month does not demonstrate it. Industry detail at the major-sector level is too coarse to isolate AI-exposed occupations, and occupational detail comes from the household survey, which has a far smaller sample and no monthly industry cross-tabs at useful precision. Nonfarm payroll change is a count of jobs added or lost, not a share of jobs displaced, so it enters jobsdata.ai as an overlay on the displacement charts rather than a data point. First-print payroll figures for 2026 have been revised substantially in both directions, so a single month's reading should be weighted lightly until its two revisions are in.
